frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network harvested credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: LSASS memory access or dumping (e.g., procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, Mimikatz), SAM/SECURITY hive or NTDS.dit extraction, credential-store or DPAPI access, Kerberoasting/AS-REP roasting, or suspicious access to lsass.exe by non-standard processes.
frame.what_would_refute: No evidence of credential-dumping tooling or LSASS/hive access, no anomalous authentication with harvested credentials, and no credential-theft artifacts across the affected Windows hosts.

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: Hands-on-keyboard credential-access campaign by pbeesly on scranton: hidden encoded PowerShell, Sysinternals accesschk, private-key/cert export, keystroke capture, clipboard theft, plus LSASS full-access handle.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: wsmprovhost.exe as pbeesly opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff on nashua.dmevals.local (Sysmon 10 and Security 4663), a new host beyond the scranton anchors; csc.exe Add-Type compilation preceded it on scranton.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: Only lsass.exe itself (SCRANTON$) opened SAM_SERVER/SAM_DOMAIN handles; no reg save, no SAM hive file access, no attacker process touching SAM.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow process, no ntds.dit file creation or modification, no PowerShell referencing ntds.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: Only routine LOCAL SERVICE queries of Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC; no SECURITY hive or Policy\Secrets object access by any other principal.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: No object access on SECURITY/Cache objects and no PowerShell referencing cache/secretsdump.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: Single DS-Replication-Get-Changes GUID access on newyork by the DC's own machine account NEWYORK$; no DRSUAPI/lsadump/dcsync tooling or script blocks.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: Only capture activity is a short netsh trace start/stop on scranton.dmevals.local spawned by the Azure Network Watcher agent (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service) as SYSTEM, writing an ETL to the agent's TEMP GUID folder — expected cloud monitoring behaviour. No pktmon/dumpcap/windump/tcpdump/RawCap/Npcap/WinPcap executions, no pcap/npf driver image loads, no capture-driver service installs, and no promiscuous/monitor/sniff command lines in Sysmon, Security or PowerShell telemetry; zeek notices are only self-signed TLS certificate validation failures.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Input/credential capture tooling present on scranton: PowerShell toolkit (Get-PrivateKeys certificate export, Invoke-Exfil) plus full-access lsass handle; other lsass access is benign system/agent activity.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: No keylogger processes, keyboard-hook script blocks, or keyboard filter driver installs; registry 'Keyboard' hits are benign CTF KeyboardLayout values written by LogonUI/winlogon.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: Only legitimate consent.exe UAC processes and DSC/AD PSCredential parameter bindings; no fake credential prompt or GUI capture.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No IIS/w3wp/appcmd activity or wwwroot/inetpub access in Windows telemetry; zeek window does not overlap.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, pbeesly) on scranton opened lsass with 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff with an UNKNOWN-module call trace, corroborated by 4656/4663 lsass access events.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625/4771 failures in windows.security and windows.other; all 297 4624 logons successful. Credential access on scranton was lsass memory access (0x1FFFFF by PowerShell.exe), not brute force.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No failed logons and no brute-force/4625-referencing script blocks; password-keyword 4104 hits are certificate export and 7-Zip archive passwords.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: No hashcat/secretsdump/Mimikatz/NTDS tooling or hive file writes; SAM/NTDS handle requests come only from lsass.exe itself and the 16962 event is an informational SAM restriction notice.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No failure spikes; repeated 4648 logons for pbeesly correlate with four PSEXESVC service installs on nashua, i.e. psexec remote execution, not spraying.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed authentications and no credential-list replay tooling; net/runas command lines are svchost/netsh noise and one benign hostui.exe runas.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/credential-provider interception evidence: zero registry writes to SecurityProviders, no fake credential/MFA provider service (only javamtsup.exe and PSEXESVC installs by pbeesly), no MFA/token-harvesting script blocks. The high-access lsass handle opens (PowerShell.exe 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff on scranton, wsmprovhost.exe 0x1f3fff on nashua) follow Sysinternals accesschk token-attribute enumeration and PowerShell remoting, and the 4648 events are pbeesly's own credentials to NASHUA over SMB plus routine DWM/UMFD/machine-account logons - consistent with credential/token enumeration and lateral movement, not MFA interception.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: No forced-authentication activity: SMB (445/139) traffic is only System-process connections between known internal hosts (10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.4/5/6/10, link-local fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429) and share access is limited to IPC$/SYSVOL/ADMIN$ by machine accounts and pbeesly; no attacker-controlled share, no WebDAV/NTLM coercion script blocks (4104 check empty). The hostui.lnk dropped into the StartUp folder on scranton is suspicious persistence/execution activity but no evidence it points to a remote UNC/WebDAV resource to harvest credentials.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe running as DMEVALS\pbeesly opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF (read-from-process-memory, duplicate-handle) at 03:05:16Z, with an UNKNOWN-module call trace, inside an interactive session that also ran Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, accesschk, Get-PrivateKeys/Export-PfxCertificate, screen capture and clipboard/keystroke collection. No named dumping tool (Mimikatz) or dump file was observed and the 4104 log has a gap over the exact command, so the LSASS access is suspicious rather than proven credential theft. The nashua wsmprovhost LSASS handle is explained by Get-Process -IncludeUserName, and the remaining svchost/wininit/csrss/Azure-agent handles are OS baseline.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Cleartext domain password 'Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by' embedded in PsExec64 command lines used from scranton to authenticate to nashua.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: python.exe payload on nashua enumerated the user profile for *pass*/*psw*/*login*/*sifr*/*vpn*/*.pst files and archived them into a password-protected RAR; accesschk.exe wrote passwordsDB on scranton.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All Password/Credential registry writes came from svchost, lsass, services and winlogon; no reg query/save or SAM/SECURITY access.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No ConsoleHost_history, PSReadLine or Get-History activity in script blocks, command lines or file creation.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported all LocalMachine certificates to C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx via Export-PfxCertificate on scranton.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: No Groups.xml, cpassword, gpprefdecrypt or SYSVOL access in PowerShell, process, SMB 5145 or file-create telemetry.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: All lsass handle events are routine service access (svchost 0x1000, telemetry/AV 0x1400, boot-time wininit/csrss) or PowerShell process enumeration (get-process / Get-Process -IncludeUserName); no dumping tooling or dump command lines exist.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: No access, copy or reference to browser credential stores (Login Data, Local State, logins.json, key4.db, Cookies) in sysmon, security or PowerShell logs.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: No cmdkey/vaultcmd/CredRead activity; vaultsvc and CredentialEnrollmentManager strings are OS MuiCache/service-registration writes by services.exe.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No .kdbx files, no KeePass/1Password/LastPass processes or script references; only attacker-embedded credentials in the exfil script.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: LSASS handle opens are dominated by svchost.exe (289), Azure antimalware (15) and Azure telemetry (13); no registry/file modification of the authentication process was found.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: Only standard logon packages (Kerberos, Advapi, User32, NtLmSsp) in 4624 events; no DC authentication tampering.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: Temp DLLs on scranton are PowerShell Add-Type/csc compilations for shellcode execution; no Notification Packages registry change or LSA DLL access.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739 events and no reversible-encryption related commands; 4657 hits are WMI Autologger registry noise.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: Only routine 4662 $MACHINE.ACC reads by LOCAL SERVICE and one NEWYORK$ replication-control access; no 5136/4739 policy changes.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136 directory modifications and no non-standard authentication packages indicating hybrid-identity bypass.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No NetworkProvider registry (event 13) or file (event 11) activity; the LSASS full-access handles from PowerShell/wsmprovhost are credential dumping, not network provider registration.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: SMB (445) connections are only System-process traffic to the DC 10.0.0.4 and nashua 10.0.1.6; the sole external logon source 172.18.39.2 is the WEC collector. No host is positioned between peers.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: DNS queries are routine DC/telemetry lookups; the one wpad query from svchost returned QueryStatus 9003 with no answer, and Zeek DNS shows only NOERROR/NXDOMAIN with no redirected answers. SMB destinations are internal only.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: Only three source MACs in Zeek conn data and no MAC spanning many IPs; the 12:34:56:78:9a:bc destination MAC is a synthetic placeholder, not a real poisoning indicator.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: Zero Sysmon connections to UDP 67/68, no DHCP event codes in windows.other, no DHCP content in PowerShell logs, and no DHCP log type in Zeek.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: Only 14x4768 and 28x4769 Kerberos events, all AES (0x12), Status 0x0, PreAuthType 2, for machine accounts/krbtgt; no ticket files, no ticket-dumping tooling, no RC4 downgrade. Broad lsass access by PowerShell/wsmprovhost produced no ticket artifacts (only WerFault crash dumps).

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: krbtgt 4769 requests are legitimate AES tickets preceded by matching preauthenticated 4768 requests from the same client; no krbtgt/golden/mimikatz strings and no lsass dump artifacts.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: Service tickets are AES for machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) only; no RC4, no unusual service accounts, no silver/kirbi strings.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No RC4 service tickets, no user SPNs requested, no kerberoast/SPN/Rubeus strings, no kerberos/klist command lines; Zeek shows no TGS burst.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: All 4768 requests used PreAuthType 2 with Status 0x0; no failed TGT requests and no asreproast/GetNPUsers/DontReqPreAuth activity.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, pbeesly ran attacker tooling from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite: PowerShell opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff access, token-attribute enumeration (Get-AttributesMask), accesschk.exe, an Invoke-Exfil function that 7-Zips Downloads and copies it to \\192.168.0.4\webdav with hardcoded credentials, sdelete64.exe wiping files, and PsExec64.exe with cleartext credentials (Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) against NASHUA launching C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: rundll32 davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie for http://192.168.0.4/webdav and an INetCookies file created by svchost on SCRANTON show WebDAV credential-cookie handling tied to the attacker's exfil share, but this is a WebClient artifact of the attacker's own mapping, not a forged/stolen browser cookie replayed for impersonation.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: Zero hits for SAML/ADFS/NotOnOrAfter/token-signing in PowerShell and windows.other, no ADFS HTTP in zeek; 4624 logons are Kerberos/Advapi dominated and zeek Kerberos shows only AS/TGS requests to the DC. 4648 events are explained by the PsExec activity and routine DWM/UMFD/winlogon logons.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA/2FA/authenticator/one-time-code strings in windows.other messages or windows.powershell 4104 script blocks; no 4625 failed logons in windows.security; no auth/MFA service or process names. The flagged zeek hits are internal TLS (10.0.1.4 -> 192.168.0.5:443) and internal WebDAV HTTP (DavClnt OPTIONS / -> 403) to 192.168.0.4, with no external identity provider in DNS or TLS subjects. Malicious PowerShell tradecraft (Invoke-SeaDukeStage, Invoke-Exfil, Invoke-Persistence) by pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local is present but does not include MFA request generation.

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly's PowerShell session ran a Get-PrivateKeys function (Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) that recursively enumerated cert:\LocalMachine and exported every certificate with Export-PfxCertificate to a randomly named .pfx in Downloads protected by the hardcoded password 'saribas'; Sysmon recorded C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by powershell.exe at 03:04:57Z and deleted at 03:08:51Z by an Invoke-BeachCleanup function that wipes *.pfx/*.bmp/*.png and %APPDATA%\OfficeSupplies.7z. The export follows a hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell that IEX'd a payload decoded from monkey.png, indicating deliberate certificate private-key theft with anti-forensic cleanup. No PKINIT/certificate-based logon was observed (all 4768 TGTs PreAuthType 2, Status 0x0).

This is a hands-on-keyboard credential-access campaign; the LSASS full-access handle from the same PowerShell process is the credential-dumping step.

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976 / 0xba0) running as DMEVALS\pbeesly requested a handle to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (and a second handle with 0x1F3FFF), i.e. PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS including 'Read from process memory' and 'Duplicate handle into or out of process' — the access pattern used to read LSASS credential material. The call trace ends in UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D), i.e. code not backed by a loaded module, consistent with in-memory/reflective tooling rather than a signed dumper. This occurred inside an interactive pbeesly session that minutes earlier ran Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence -PersistStep 1/2, accesschk.exe, Get-PrivateKeys (Export-PfxCertificate of machine certs with hardcoded password 'saribas'), Invoke-ScreenCapture, Get-Clipboard and a keystroke/AV-check function, and that also staged user documents/password-named files into an archive — a credential-access and collection toolkit. No Mimikatz/Invoke-Mimikatz script block was logged (C137 zero hits), so the LSASS access is the primary T1212 evidence rather than a named dumping tool. Note the 4104 script-block log has a gap between 03:05:08 ('exit') and 03:05:25, so the exact command that opened the handle was not captured.

findings.title: Get-PrivateKeys PowerShell function exported machine certificate private keys to password-protected .pfx files on SCRANTON
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, in the session of user DMEVALS\pbeesly, a PowerShell script block named Get-PrivateKeys (ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, logged with Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) enumerated every certificate in cert:\LocalMachine recursively and called Export-PfxCertificate for each certificate with a thumbprint, writing the private-key-bearing .pfx to $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx protected by the hardcoded password "saribas". The function was invoked at 2020-05-02T03:04:56Z (script block 'Get-PrivateKeys', PID 3876) and at 03:04:57.460Z Sysmon recorded the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by powershell.exe (PID 3876). This is direct theft of authentication certificate private keys from the local machine store, matching T1649. The activity sits inside a broader intrusion chain on the same host: at 02:58:44Z a hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell (parent control.exe /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter) decoded a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png via System.Drawing pixel extraction and IEX'd it; at 03:08:51Z a second PowerShell (PID 3852) ran an Invoke-BeachCleanup function (Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1) that deleted Downloads\*.pfx, *.bmp, *.png and %APPDATA%\OfficeSupplies.7z, and Sysmon event 23 confirms coyn5igj.3io.pfx was deleted at 03:08:51.489Z by DMEVALS\pbeesly. The export-then-wipe pattern indicates deliberate exfiltration staging and anti-forensics. No certificate-based (PKINIT) authentication was observed: all 14 Kerberos 4768 TGT requests in windows.security show PreAuthType 2 (password pre-auth) with Status 0x0, and the single SystemCertificates registry modification (4657 on nashua.dmevals.local, ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656, by NASHUA$) is not linked to this activity. Zeek x509/kerberos data (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window and shows only AS/TGS requests with KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED, no certificate-auth anomalies.

verification.actual:
function Invoke-BeachCleanup {
    Write-Host "[*] Cleaning up"
    Remove-Item -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\*.pfx" -Force
    Remove-Item -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\*.bmp" -Force
    Remove-Item -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\*.png" -Force
    Remove-Item -Path "$env:APPDATA\OfficeSupplies.7z" -Force
}

PowerShell on scranton.dmevals.local drops hostui.lnk into the all-users StartUp folder (persistence, not forced authentication)
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, the PowerShell process (PID 3876, ProcessGuid {47ab858c-e23d-5eac-c603-000000000400}) first wrote C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\SysinternalsSuite\hostui.txt at 03:00:27Z and then created C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp\hostui.lnk at 03:04:23Z. Later, at 03:21:19Z, pbeesly ran 'powershell.exe -c "Start-Process C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe -verb runas"' (parent cmd.exe), and the matching 4104 script block was logged. This is a shortcut dropped into a startup location plus an elevated launch of hostui.exe — behaviour consistent with persistence/execution, but no evidence of forced authentication: the .lnk was not shown to point at a UNC/WebDAV path, and no outbound SMB/WebDAV authentication to an attacker-controlled host was observed. The two other .lnk files (Backup and Restore (Windows 7).lnk, System and Security.lnk) were created by Explorer.EXE in pbeesly's Recent folder and are normal shell artefacts.

findings.title: accesschk.exe wrote a file named passwordsDB on scranton during the intrusion
findings.summary: At 2020-05-02T03:04:35.069Z on scranton.dmevals.local, Sysmon event 11 shows C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\accesschk.exe (PID 9204) creating the file C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\passwordsDB. This occurred inside the same pbeesly intrusion session that also ran Get-PrivateKeys and Invoke-Exfil, and the file name indicates credential material being written to disk. No command line for this accesschk invocation was captured, so the exact purpose is inferred from the file name and surrounding activity rather than observed directly.

findings.title: Password filter DLL: DLLs written to user Temp are PowerShell Add-Type compilations, not LSA notification packages
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (user pbeesly) created C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Local\Temp\qkbkqqbs\qkbkqqbs.dll at 2020-05-02T02:58:45Z and C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Local\Temp\0piklvia\0piklvia.dll at 03:08:03Z, with csc.exe compiling the first one. The 02:58:45 script block (4104) shows Add-Type with kernel32 VirtualAlloc/CreateThread DllImport declarations followed by a large shellcode byte array — in-memory code execution, not a password filter. No 4657 change to 'Notification Packages', no 4663 access to LSA DLLs, and no 4104 referencing Notification/PasswordFilter/lsa were found, so no password filter was registered. The DLL writes are attacker tooling but do not implement T1556.002.

The cookie is a legitimate WebClient artifact generated by the attacker's own WebDAV mapping, not a forged/stolen browser cookie replayed to impersonate a user, so it is suspicious context rather than confirmed T1606.001 forgery. No browser cookie stores were touched and no PowerShell referenced cookie theft.

netsh trace packet capture on scranton.dmevals.local is Azure Network Watcher agent telemetry, not adversary sniffing
findings.summary: The only packet-capture activity in the Windows telemetry is a single netsh trace session on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z: 'netsh.exe trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-DFE6-43C7-8FA8-8D3AC5AA8726\B91E06C5-1C7C-4830-9A76-74FA211560A7.etl"' followed ~7 seconds later by 'netsh.exe trace stop'. Both Security 4688 and Sysmon event 1 show the creator/parent process as C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\NetworkWatcherAgent.exe (command line "...NetworkWatcherAgent.exe" /service), running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM with LogonId 0x3e7. This is the documented Azure Network Watcher packet-capture extension behaviour (short-lived ETL capture in the agent's TEMP GUID folder), not interactive attacker use. No other capture tooling was found: no pktmon/dumpcap/windump/tcpdump/RawCap/Npcap/WinPcap command lines in Sysmon or Security 4688, no pcap/npf/Packet driver image loads (Sysmon event 6), no capture-driver service installs (7045), and no promiscuous/monitor/sniff command lines. The 7045 service installs in the window are unrelated (Java(TM) Virtual Machine Support Service via javamtsup.exe on scranton, and repeated PSEXESVC installs on nashua by user pbeesly), none of which are packet-capture drivers. In the non-overlapping zeek window (2020-04-30) the only notices are SSL::Invalid_Server_Cert self-signed certificate validation failures from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.5:443 and 10.0.1.6 to 192.168.0.4:8443, with no sniffing-related notice or weird entries indicating a sniffer on the wire.

The bulk of the 326 lsass handle opens in the window are routine: svchost.exe (289 events, GrantedAccess 0x1000/0x101001 with call traces through lsm.dll), WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe (13 events, 0x1400 via CorperfmonExt.dll performance counters), AntimalwareConfig.exe (15), wininit.exe/csrss.exe at boot (0x1fffff/0x1000000), CollectGuestLogs.exe and MsMpEng.exe (0x10 read-attributes). No keylogger driver, no input-capture service, and no GUI/web-portal capture artifacts were observed; the only anomalous lsass access is the PowerShell full-access pair reported under T1056.004. The 7045 service installs (javamtsup.exe on scranton, PSEXESVC on nashua) are not input-capture tooling.
findings.title: Benign lsass handle activity by system services and Azure agents (no input-capture tooling found)

No brute-force authentication activity; credential theft on scranton was lsass memory access, not password guessing
findings.summary: Across windows.security (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) there are zero 4625 failed-logon events, zero 4771 and only one 4776 (a success, Status 0x0, for pbeesly on newyork at 23:20:40 local). All 297 4624 logons are successful and dominated by machine accounts (NEWYORK$ 123, SCRANTON$ 37, NASHUA$ 25) plus pbeesly (30). No repeated authentication attempts, no failure bursts, no password-guessing tooling. The credential access that did occur on scranton.dmevals.local was PowerShell.exe opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF / 0x1F3FFF at 03:05:16Z (a memory-dump access mask, T1003.001 territory), which is outside the T1110 family. The single 'net user/password' command-line hit (C097) and the 'net use/runas' hit (C119) resolve to a benign Start-Process hostui.exe -verb runas and svchost/netsh noise, not scripted authentication.

findings.title: No password guessing: zero 4625 failures and no brute-force script blocks
findings.summary: Checks C099-C104 returned no 4625 events in windows.security or windows.other, and no PowerShell script block referencing 4625/Failed Logon/Brute. The only 4104 blocks matching password/credential keywords are unrelated: a Get-PrivateKeys certificate-export function with a hardcoded string on scranton (pbeesly, 23:04:56), an Invoke-Exfil 7-Zip archive password on scranton (23:08:02), and AD-cmdlet help text on newyork. None of these generate repeated logon attempts. The 4648 explicit-credential logons for pbeesly (9) are psexec-driven remote execution, not guessing.

findings.title: lsass handle access by PowerShell is memory dumping, not offline password cracking
findings.summary: C106/C107/C110/C112 hits are explained by legitimate or non-cracking behaviour: the 10 handle requests to SAM/SECURITY/NTDS objects come solely from C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe itself, 4670 permission changes are services.exe/svchost.exe/SearchIndexer.exe housekeeping, and the single SAM-related windows.other event is the informational 16962 'Remote calls to the SAM database are being restricted' message on scranton. No hashcat/secretsdump/Invoke-Mimikatz/NTDS script blocks (C111) and no SAM/NTDS/.dit/.hiv file writes (C109). The high-privilege lsass opens (0x1FFFFF by PowerShell.exe pid 2976 on scranton at 03:05:16Z, 0x1F3FFF by wsmprovhost.exe on nashua at 03:09:29Z) indicate in-memory credential theft (T1003.001), not password cracking, so no T1110.002 activity is present.

findings.title: No password spraying: no failure spikes, 4648 logons are psexec remote execution
findings.summary: C113-C117 found no 4625/4771 events at all, so there is no spray pattern (no many-users-one-password failure burst). The 4648 explicit-credential events for pbeesly alternate between scranton (IpAddress 10.0.1.6) and nashua (ProcessName C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe, SubjectUserName NASHUA$) every ~20-60s between 23:11 and 23:15 local, matching four PSEXESVC service installs on nashua (7045, 23:11:39-23:15:03) — i.e. repeated psexec remote execution with known credentials, not spraying. Remaining 4648s are DWM-*/UMFD-*/SCRANTON$ logon-session noise from winlogon/wininit/taskhostw.

findings.title: No credential stuffing: no failed logons and no credential-replay tooling
findings.summary: C302-C307 returned no 4625/4771/4776 failure events. The C305 'net/runas/psexec' command-line stack is 28 svchost.exe and 2 netsh.exe events plus one benign runas of hostui.exe, none of which replay stolen credential lists. The 4104 credential-keyword blocks (C306) are the certificate-export and 7-Zip exfil functions on scranton, which use a single hardcoded string rather than a credential list. The only successful 4776 (pbeesly, newyork, 23:20:40) is a single NTLM validation, not stuffing.

findings.title: No MFA/credential-provider interception artifacts; lsass handle opens traced to Sysinternals accesschk token enumeration and PowerShell remoting
findings.summary: Hunting for T1111 (MFA interception) on 2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z across scranton/nashua/newyork/utica found no MFA-provider or credential-interception artifacts: no registry writes to SecurityProviders (C123 zero hits), no new service resembling a fake credential/MFA provider (the only 7045 installs are javamtsup.exe on scranton and repeated PSEXESVC on nashua, both installed by pbeesly), and no script block referencing MFA/token theft. The high-access lsass handle opens that could look like credential/MFA-secret reads are explainable: on scranton, PowerShell.exe (pid 2976) opened lsass with 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff at 03:05:16, immediately after pbeesly ran C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\accessChk.exe (03:04:34) and the Sysinternals readme.ps1 script block that enumerates access-token group attributes (SE_GROUP_LOGON_ID etc.) - i.e. token/privilege enumeration, not MFA interception. On nashua, wsmprovhost.exe opened lsass with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29 with a call trace through Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll, consistent with a PowerShell remoting session (the same pbeesly PSEXESVC/4648 activity at 03:11-03:15). The remaining lsass opens are OS components (wininit.exe, csrss.exe, svchost.exe via lsm.dll/sysmain.dll, AntimalwareConfig.exe and WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe with 0x1400). The 4648 explicit-credential events are pbeesly re-using its own credentials to NASHUA over SMB (10.0.1.6:445) and PSEXESVC localhost logons, plus routine DWM/UMFD/winlogon and taskhostw machine-account logons - no alternate-credential or token theft. Note: the environment does show other malicious activity (an Invoke-Exfil script block on scranton using a hardcoded PSCredential for a WebDAV share at \\192.168.0.4\webdav), but that is credential use/exfiltration, not MFA interception.

findings.title: SMB traffic in the Windows window is normal domain administration (ADMIN$/IPC$/SYSVOL) between known internal hosts
findings.summary: All 66 Sysmon network events to ports 445/139 are System-process SMB connections between known internal addresses: newyork.dmevals.local to 10.0.0.4 and to link-local fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429, nashua/scranton to 10.0.1.6 and 10.0.0.4, utica to 10.0.0.4. The 42 Security 5140 share-access events are only \\*\IPC$, \\*\SYSVOL and \\*\ADMIN$ from machine accounts (SCRANTON$, NASHUA$, UTICA$, WEC$) and user pbeesly from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.5/10.0.1.6/10.0.1.10 — standard domain logon-script/SYSVOL and admin-share access, with no attacker-controlled share or external SMB endpoint. The Zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window; its SMB connections are 10.0.1.4 -> 10.0.1.6:445 (30), 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6 -> 10.0.0.4:445 (10) and 10.0.1.4 -> 192.168.0.4:445 (10), all internal, with no WebDAV (80/443 to a UNC-style host) coercion observed. No 4104 script block referencing WebDAV or NTLM was found.

findings.title: wsmprovhost.exe LSASS handle on nashua.dmevals.local explained by Get-Process -IncludeUserName
findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:09:29Z, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF, which at first looks like credential dumping. The call trace is entirely managed code (System.ni.dll and Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll), and the PowerShell 4104 script block logged one second earlier in the same pbeesly session is 'Get-Process -IncludeUserName | Select-Object UserName,SessionId | Where-Object { $_.UserName -like "*\$env:USERNAME" }'. Get-Process -IncludeUserName resolves each process owner via LSASS, which produces exactly this handle. No memory-read tooling, no dump file, and no further LSASS access followed.

findings.title: No Windows Credential Manager / Vault harvesting; vaultsvc references are OS service registration

findings.summary: Across 297 event 4624 logons the LogonProcessName values are Kerberos (217), Advapi (76), User32 (2), NtLmSsp (1) and '-' (1) — all standard Windows authentication packages, with no custom or injected package. Network logons (4624 type 3) target machine accounts NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$, UTICA$, WEC$ and user pbeesly, consistent with normal domain traffic. No 4104 script block or windows.other message referenced lsass/cryptdll/mimikatz. No DC authentication tampering observed.

findings.title: Reversible encryption: no account-control or policy changes; 4657 hits are WMI Autologger registry noise

The 36 event 4657 registry modifications are dominated by \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\WMI\Autologger\EventLog-Application\{GUID} keys plus a SystemCertificates entry and WSMAN SafeClientList — routine system configuration, not account encryption settings.

findings.title: MFA modification: no authentication-policy object changes; 4662 SecretObject reads are LOCAL SERVICE machine-account access

Six are 4662 reads of Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC (ObjectType SecretObject, AccessMask 0x2) by LOCAL SERVICE on nashua, scranton and utica — normal machine-account secret access. The seventh is a 4662 by NEWYORK$ on newyork.dmevals.local at 2020-05-01T23:16:15Z against object %{11487126-e2dc-4f51-acb1-1b0df0573bb5} with AccessMask 0x100 and properties listing {1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2} and {19195a5b-6da0-11d0-afd3-00c04fd930c9} (directory-service replication/DS-Replication-Get-Changes control access). No 4739 and no 5136 directory modifications were recorded, so no MFA/authentication policy was altered.

findings.title: Hybrid identity: no federation/token-signing or directory changes; logon packages all standard
findings.summary: No 5136 directory-service modifications were recorded at all, and the 4624 LogonProcessName distribution (Kerberos 217, Advapi 76, User32 2, NtLmSsp 1, '-' 1) shows no non-standard authentication package that would indicate a hybrid-identity/PTA or token-signing bypass. The 20,259 image-load events are overwhelmingly stock System32 DLLs (ntdll.dll, KernelBase.dll, kernel32.dll, rpcrt4.dll, sechost.dll ...); no unusual identity-provider DLL was identified.

findings.title: No adversary-in-the-middle positioning observed; SMB/DNS traffic is normal domain traffic
findings.summary: Across the 2020-05-02 Windows window (02:55-03:28Z) and the 2020-04-30 Zeek window (00:06-00:45Z) there is no evidence of a host positioned between peers. All Sysmon 3 SMB (445) connections are made by the System process to the domain controller 10.0.0.4 and to nashua 10.0.1.6, i.e. ordinary domain/SMB traffic, not relay to an attacker host. Zeek conn records show only three source MACs (00:0d:3a:13:e3:69, 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2, fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) and the destination MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a synthetic placeholder value, not a duplicated real MAC spanning many IPs. The only non-internal network logon source, 172.18.39.2, is the WEC collector (win.host wec.internal.cloudapp.net) authenticating pbeesly with NTLM V2, which is expected log forwarding. Note: the malicious javamtsup.exe service on scranton is execution/persistence activity, not AiTM.

findings.title: Name resolution and SMB authentication show no poisoning or relay; wpad query failed with no answer
findings.summary: Sysmon 22 DNS queries on the Windows hosts are routine: DC/service discovery (_ldap._tcp..., NEWYORK/SCRANTON/NASHUA), Microsoft telemetry and update endpoints, and reverse lookups. The single 'wpad' query on scranton came from svchost.exe (SYSTEM) and returned QueryStatus 9003 with no results, so no rogue WPAD/proxy answer was delivered. The '..localmachine' queries from spoolsv.exe resolved to the legitimate host address 10.0.1.4. Zeek DNS shows only NOERROR (25) and NXDOMAIN (12) responses with no anomalous answer redirection, and SMB (445) destinations are limited to 10.0.1.6, 10.0.0.4 and 192.168.0.4. The odd DNS-querying binary C:\ProgramData\victim\â€®cod.3aka3.scr on scranton only resolved its own host name and its own IPv6 PTR, which is not name-resolution poisoning.

findings.title: No ARP cache poisoning indicators; MAC-to-IP mapping is consistent
findings.summary: Zeek conn records in the 2020-04-30 window contain only three distinct source MAC addresses and no single MAC appearing across many unrelated IPs, which is the hallmark of ARP cache poisoning. The dominant destination MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a synthetic placeholder value present on 559 records, not a real attacker NIC claiming multiple IPs. Host-to-host flows stay on their expected paths (10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6 to the DC 10.0.0.4, plus broadcast to 10.0.1.255), with no evidence of traffic being redirected through an unexpected peer.

findings.title: No Kerberos ticket theft or forgery observed; all Kerberos traffic is normal AES/preauth traffic
findings.summary: Across windows.security (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) the only Kerberos events are 14x 4768 and 28x 4769, all on newyork.dmevals.local, all with TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256), Status 0x0 and PreAuthType 2. Service tickets are requested only for machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt by pbeesly/SCRANTON$ from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6 - ordinary workstation-to-DC ticket acquisition, no RC4 downgrade, no anomalous SPN sweep. The only lsass access with broad rights came from PowerShell.exe (0x1fffff/0x1f3fff) on scranton and wsmprovhost.exe (0x1f3fff) on nashua, but no ticket/hash artifacts followed: no .kirbi/.ccache files, no sekurlsa/klist/rubeus/kerberos command lines, and the only dumps written were WerFault crash dumps. The PowerShell 800 event that matched 'lsass' was merely a Get-Process listing. Zeek (2020-04-30, non-overlapping window) shows 14 AS and 11 TGS requests with no roasting burst.

findings.title: No golden ticket indicators: krbtgt tickets are legitimate AES TGT-service requests
findings.summary: The 3 krbtgt service-ticket requests (4769) on newyork.dmevals.local at 2020-05-01T23:04:04, 23:19:13 and 23:19:15 local time are for pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL and SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL, all AES (0x12), Status 0x0, TicketOptions 0x60810010, and each is preceded by a matching 4768 TGT request with PreAuthType 2 from the same client (10.0.1.4) - i.e. normal TGT renewal/service use, not forged tickets. No krbtgt/golden/mimikatz strings in PowerShell or other Windows channels, and no lsass dump artifacts. The PowerShell 800 hit was a benign Get-Process output listing.

findings.title: No silver ticket indicators: service tickets are AES for machine accounts only
findings.summary: All 28 TGS requests on newyork.dmevals.local target machine accounts (NEWYORK$ 11, NASHUA$ 10, SCRANTON$ 3, WEC$ 1) plus krbtgt 3, all encrypted with 0x12 (AES) and Status 0x0, requested by pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL or SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6. No RC4 (0x17) service tickets, no unusual service accounts, and no silver/ticket/kirbi strings in PowerShell. The wsmprovhost.exe lsass access on nashua (0x1f3fff) has a call trace through System.ni.dll / Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll, consistent with PowerShell remoting activity rather than a service-account hash dump, and no ticket files were written.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting: no RC4 service tickets and no SPN enumeration
findings.summary: Kerberoasting requires RC4-encrypted TGS replies for user/service accounts. All 28 4769 events carry TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256) and Status 0x0, and the requested services are only machine accounts and krbtgt - no user SPNs were requested. No kerberoast/Invoke-Kerberoast/SPN/Rubeus strings appear in PowerShell or other Windows channels, and no kerberos/ticket/klist command lines exist in Sysmon process creation. Zeek kerberos logs (2020-04-30, separate window) show 14 AS and 11 TGS requests, no roasting burst.

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting: all TGT requests used preauthentication and succeeded
findings.summary: All 14 4768 events on newyork.dmevals.local have PreAuthType 2 (preauthentication required) and Status 0x0, for pbeesly (9) and SCRANTON$ (5) from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6. There are no failed TGT requests (no 0x18/0x25 statuses) and no asreproast/GetNPUsers/DontReqPreAuth strings in Sysmon command lines, PowerShell or other Windows channels, so no account without preauthentication was targeted.

findings.title: No SAML/token-signing forgery observed; Kerberos and logon activity is ordinary domain authentication
findings.summary: No evidence of forged SAML tokens or token-signing certificate abuse. Searches for SAML/ADFS/NotOnOrAfter/token-signing strings in PowerShell script blocks and windows.other messages returned zero hits, and no HTTP traffic to an ADFS endpoint exists in the zeek window. The 297 successful 4624 logons are dominated by Kerberos (217) and Advapi (76) with only 2 User32 and 1 NtLmSsp, and the zeek Kerberos records are only AS (14) and TGS (11) requests between 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6 and the DC 10.0.0.4 — normal domain authentication. The 4648 explicit-credential events are explained by the attacker's PsExec usage (pbeesly to NASHUA, PSEXESVC.exe on nashua) and by routine DWM/UMFD/winlogon localhost logons, not by forged federated tokens. Note the zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows telemetry (2020-05-02), so network-side SAML use cannot be fully excluded.

findings.title: No MFA request generation observed; zeek hits are internal WebDAV and internal TLS traffic
findings.summary: The two zeek hits flagged for T1621 are not MFA-related. The 443 connections are internal host-to-host TLS flows from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.5 (zeek service 'ssl', conn_state SF, 437 bytes out / 204450 bytes in) observed by simplerockbuild.simplerock.lan on 2020-04-30T00:15:18Z. The 62 HTTP records all go to a single internal destination 192.168.0.4 on port 80; the sampled event is a WebDAV client (user_agent 'DavClnt') OPTIONS / request answered 403 Forbidden. No external identity/MFA provider (e.g. Okta, Azure AD, Duo) appears in DNS or TLS server names, and no MFA/2FA/authenticator/one-time-code strings exist in windows.other messages or windows.powershell 4104 script blocks. Windows security shows no 4625 failed logons at all and no authentication-service processes or objects matching auth/mfa. The genuine malicious activity in this window (pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local running Invoke-SeaDukeStage, Invoke-Exfil, Invoke-Persistence, Invoke-ScreenCapture) is credential-access-adjacent tradecraft but contains no MFA prompt generation, so T1621 is not observed.

findings.title: No DHCP spoofing activity; no DHCP traffic or DHCP-related events present
findings.summary: No DHCP spoofing indicators exist in any dataset. A Sysmon 3 search for UDP ports 67/68 returned zero rows, so no host contacted or impersonated a DHCP server. The windows.other System channel contains no DHCP-server/client event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063 returned zero hits), windows.powershell has no DHCP-related content, and Zeek UDP log types are limited to conn and dns with no DHCP log. The only UDP service ports observed are 53, 138, 123, 137, 389 and 1900, all normal.

incidents.title: PowerShell full-access LSASS handle on scranton (credential dumping / in-memory theft)
incidents.rationale: F01, F09, F22 and F41 all describe the same 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z event on scranton where PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, pbeesly) opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff and an UNKNOWN call trace; F60 covers the csc.exe Add-Type compilation in the same hidden PowerShell chain that precedes the LSASS access. Best fit is LSASS memory credential dumping (T1003.001); the network-provider and API-hooking framings in F41/F09 are not supported by registry/file evidence.

incidents.title: wsmprovhost.exe full-access LSASS handle on nashua
incidents.rationale: WinRM host process running as pbeesly opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff (VM_READ) from managed code on nashua — LSASS memory credential dumping.

incidents.title: sdclt.exe (UAC-bypass binary) launched from cmd.exe on scranton just before the credential-access tooling
incidents.rationale: not grouped by the consolidation step

incidents.title: Hardcoded plaintext credentials in attacker PowerShell tooling on scranton
incidents.rationale: Invoke-Exfil and Get-PrivateKeys scripts embed plaintext credentials ('cozy'/'MyCozyPassw0rd!', 'saribas') — unsecured credentials in tooling.

incidents.title: accesschk.exe wrote passwordsDB on scranton
incidents.rationale: F26 and F59 cover the same accesschk.exe invocation (03:04:34-35Z) writing C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\passwordsDB — credential material written to a file, i.e. credentials in files.

incidents.title: PsExec64 with cleartext domain password from scranton to nashua
incidents.rationale: F57 and F58 describe the same PsExec64 command line embedding the plaintext dmevals\pbeesly password used to authenticate to nashua; F51 is the same pbeesly tooling chain on scranton including that PsExec64 cleartext credential. The credential-access-relevant action is the cleartext credential in the command line (T1552.001); the resulting remote execution is lateral movement.

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys exported machine certificate private keys to password-protected .pfx on scranton
incidents.rationale: F25 and F55 describe the same Get-PrivateKeys script block (readme.ps1) enumerating cert:\LocalMachine and calling Export-PfxCertificate to Downloads\<random>.pfx with hardcoded password 'saribas'. This is theft of authentication certificate private keys (T1649), which fits better than the generic private-keys technique.

incidents.title: DLLs written to user Temp are Add-Type compilations, not password filter DLLs
incidents.rationale: The finding itself concludes these Temp DLLs are PowerShell Add-Type compilations for in-memory code execution, not LSA notification packages; no password-filter modification occurred, so this is not credential access.

incidents.title: WebDAV cookie creation (DavSetCookie) on scranton
incidents.rationale: DavSetCookie/INetCookies artifacts are the WebDAV client storing an auth cookie for the exfil share; this is ingress-tool transfer/exfil channel use, not forged web session credentials.

incidents.title: hostui.lnk dropped into all-users StartUp folder on scranton
incidents.rationale: The finding describes a shortcut dropped into the StartUp folder and later run with -verb runas — persistence/elevation, not forced authentication.
